content: When an individual engages in anal sex, it is critical to differentiate between anorectal infections and other diseases. Additionally, thresholds for initiating treatment for herpes simplex virus (HSV), lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), or syphilis must be carefully considered. The selection of medications, their dosages, and the duration of treatment for anorectal infections generally align with those used for infections at other anatomical sites. For anorectal infections, the following treatment regimens are recommended: 1. Chlamydia: Doxycycline 100 mg taken orally twice daily for seven days. If nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) confirms Chlamydia trachomatis and LGV is suspected, the treatment duration should be extended to 21 days. Alternatively, a single dose of azithromycin 1 g can be used. 2. Gonorrhea: A single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg combined with a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g is the first-line treatment. Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose, combined with azithromycin 1 g orally, is an effective substitute. 3. HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus): If indicated, treatment options include acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir. For recurrent infections, acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for five days, or alternative regimens such as acyclovir 800 mg orally three times daily for two days, may be used. Valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily for three days is another option. For primary genital herpes, acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 10 days or valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 10 days is recommended. Suppressive therapy for recurrent herpes includes acyclovir 400 mg orally twice daily or valacyclovir 500 mg once daily. 4. Syphilis: For individuals with a positive syphilis test but no ulcers, benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly as a single dose is recommended. For late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, the same dose should be administered weekly for three weeks. Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days or erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 14 days are alternatives. If syphilis serology is positive, treatment may need to be extended to 30 days. If ulcerations are observed, the treatment should follow the flow chart for genital ulcers, and management for syphilis and/or LGV should be considered. The World Health Organization (WHO) is revising treatment recommendations and dosages for gonorrhea due to increasing antimicrobial resistance to azithromycin and reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins. Updated syndromic guidelines will be disseminated through printed publications, downloadable documents, and electronic media. WHO will collaborate with regional and national partners, including NGOs and UN agencies, to ensure the integration of these guidelines into sexual and reproductive health services. Efforts will also focus on improving STI surveillance, particularly in key populations, and addressing challenges such as the asymptomatic nature of many STIs, limited laboratory testing, and antimicrobial resistance. Research priorities include understanding the role of Mycoplasma genitalium in urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and proctitis, as well as the resurgence of LGV among men who have sex with men. Development of affordable diagnostic tools and validation of treatment flow charts are also critical areas of focus. Finally, WHO emphasizes the importance of capacity-building for STI surveillance, strengthening laboratories, and advocating for funding to support rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests.
